sections.title: Advanced Concept: Handling Irrationals and Huge Numbers
sections.content: Level 3 questions involve coefficients with square roots (e.g., x² - 5√3x + 18 = 0) or massive constants (e.g., x² - 84x + 1728 = 0). These require specialized splitting techniques and prime factorization methods.

sections.title: Equations with Square Roots in the Middle Term
sections.content: When 'b' contains a square root (like √3), the normal factorization method fails mentally. The trick is to divide the constant term 'c' by the number inside the root. Then factorize the resulting number normally, and attach the root to both factors.

sections.title: Equations with Large Constant Terms
sections.content: For massive 'c' values (e.g., 2552), don't guess blindly. Use prime factorization or the LCM method. Alternatively, find the nearest perfect square to the constant to estimate the middle factors.

sections.title: Higher Power Equations (Cubes & Squares)
sections.content: Exams often mix quadratic equations with cubic ones (e.g., x³ = 1331, y² = 121). Remember the Power Parity Rule: Even powers (y², y⁴) yield TWO roots (positive and negative). Odd powers (x³, x⁵) yield ONE root carrying the sign of the original number.

sections.title: Simultaneous Linear Equations in Quadratic Sets
sections.content: Sometimes, instead of two quadratics, you get two linear equations (e.g., 3x + 2y = 12, 4x - 5y = 17). Solve these using standard elimination or substitution to find single definite values for x and y, then compare them.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Treating y = √144 as y = +12, -12 (it is strictly +12; only y² = 144 gives ±12). 2. Getting intimidated by large numbers and skipping the question. 3. Forgetting to attach the square root back to the factors in root-based quadratics.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: Level 3 separates the top percentiles. Master the 'Root Division' trick for irrational coefficients. Use prime factorization for large numbers. Never fall for the x² vs √x trap regarding the number of root signs.

tricks.title: The Root Division Trick (Irrational 'b')
tricks.explanation: If equation is x² - 5√3x + 18 = 0. Step 1: Remove √3 by dividing the constant (18) by the number inside the root (3). 18/3 = 6. Step 2: Factorize x² - 5x + 6 = 0. Factors are 3, 2. Step 3: Attach √3 back. Roots are +3√3, +2√3.
tricks.example: y² - 8√2y + 30 = 0. Divide 30 by 2 = 15. Factors of 15 adding to 8 are 5, 3. Attach √2. Roots: +5√2, +3√2.

tricks.title: Large Number Factorization (Nearest Square Method)
tricks.explanation: If you have x² - 72x + 1295 = 0. Finding factors of 1295 is hard. Instead, halve the middle term (72/2 = 36). 36² = 1296. Since 1295 is just 1 less than 1296, the factors are (36-1) and (36+1) -> 35 and 37.
tricks.example: Factors of 1295 adding to 72 are 35 and 37. Roots: +35, +37.

tricks.title: The Odd/Even Power Comparison Trap
tricks.explanation: x³ = Positive Number gives ONE positive root. y² = Positive Number gives TWO roots (+ and -). If x³ = 343 (x=7) and y² = 49 (y=+7, -7). Comparison: 7=7, 7>-7. Answer: x ≥ y.

tricks.title: Difference of Squares Factorization
tricks.explanation: If the equation looks like x² - 17x = 0 (no constant term), don't use quadratic formulas. Factoring x(x - 17) = 0 gives roots x = 0 and x = 17 instantly.
tricks.example: Always check for a missing 'c' term. If c=0, one root is ALWAYS 0.
